claim: Titin is the largest protein known, with a molecular weight of approximately 3800 kDa.
source: The focus of the present study is on titin, the largest known protein (~3800 kDa), that forms the third myofilament type (Wang et al., 1984; Granzier and Labeit, 2005), spanning the half-sarcomere from Z-disk to M-band (Fürst et al., 1988).
evidence: The manuscript directly states titin's molecular weight and cites supporting literature (Wang et al., 1984; Granzier and Labeit, 2005).

claim: Titin forms an elastic myofilament that spans the half-sarcomere from Z-disk to M-band.
source: The focus of the present study is on titin, the largest known protein (~3800 kDa), that forms the third myofilament type (Wang et al., 1984; Granzier and Labeit, 2005), spanning the half-sarcomere from Z-disk to M-band (Fürst et al., 1988).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states titin's location in the sarcomere with citation support (Fürst et al., 1988).

claim: The I-band region of titin functions as a molecular spring that extends and generates passive force when muscles are stretched.
source: The I-band region of titin functions as a molecular spring that extends and generates force (passive force) when muscles are stretched (Trombitás et al., 1995).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this function with citation support (Trombitás et al., 1995).

claim: Titin's molecular spring consists of two main sub-segments: the tandem Ig segment and the PEVK segment.
source: Titin's molecular spring consists of two main sub-segments, the tandem Ig segment (serially-linked immunoglobulin (Ig)-like domains) and the PEVK segment (rich in proline (P), glutamate (E), valine (V), and lysine(K)) (Trombitás et al., 1998a; Bang et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the two main segments with citation support (Trombitás et al., 1998a; Bang et al., 2001).

claim: The tandem Ig segment and PEVK segment have different biophysical properties and their extensions dominate at different physiological sarcomere length ranges.
source: These segments have different biophysical properties and therefore their extensions dominate at different but physiological sarcomere length ranges (Trombitás et al., 1998b; Watanabe et al., 2002a).
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation support (Trombitás et al., 1998b; Watanabe et al., 2002a).

claim: Titin's force maintains the structural integrity of the sarcomere.
source: Titin's force maintains the structural integrity of the sarcomere (Horowits and Podolsky, 1987) and limits sarcomere length variation along myofibrils (serially-linked sarcomeres) (Granzier and Pollack, 1990).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this function with citation support (Horowits and Podolsky, 1987).

claim: Titin limits sarcomere length variation along myofibrils.
source: Titin's force maintains the structural integrity of the sarcomere (Horowits and Podolsky, 1987) and limits sarcomere length variation along myofibrils (serially-linked sarcomeres) (Granzier and Pollack, 1990).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this function with citation support (Granzier and Pollack, 1990).

claim: The contribution of titin to sarcomere passive stiffness in single fibers is widely accepted.
source: While the contribution of titin to sarcomere passive stiffness (slope of the passive force-sarcomere length relation) in single fibers is widely accepted (Granzier and Wang, 1993; Granzier and Labeit, 2006; Prado et al., 2005), there are conflicting views on the relevance of titin to passive stiffness at the skeletal muscle level.
evidence: The manuscript states this is widely accepted with citation support (Granzier and Wang, 1993; Granzier and Labeit, 2006; Prado et al., 2005).

claim: There are conflicting views on the relevance of titin to passive stiffness at the skeletal muscle level.
source: While the contribution of titin to sarcomere passive stiffness (slope of the passive force-sarcomere length relation) in single fibers is widely accepted (Granzier and Wang, 1993; Granzier and Labeit, 2006; Prado et al., 2005), there are conflicting views on the relevance of titin to passive stiffness at the skeletal muscle level.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states there are conflicting views.

claim: It has been proposed that the extracellular matrix dominates whole muscle passive stiffness and that titin is less relevant at the whole muscle level.
source: It has been proposed that the extracellular matrix (ECM) dominates whole muscle passive stiffness and that titin is less relevant at the whole muscle level (Prado et al., 2005; Gillies et al., 2011; Lieber et al., 2017; Tirrell et al., 2012; Meyer and Lieber, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies proposing this view (Prado et al., 2005; Gillies et al., 2011; Lieber et al., 2017; Tirrell et al., 2012; Meyer and Lieber, 2011).

claim: Studies have concluded that the passive stiffness of whole muscle fully resides in single fibers (titin).
source: This contrasts with studies that concluded that the passive stiffness of whole muscle fully resides in single fibers (titin) (Magid and Law, 1985) and also with work on cardiac muscle, where titin's stiffness exceeds ECM-stiffness (Granzier and Irving, 1995; Wu et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study supporting this view (Magid and Law, 1985).

claim: In cardiac muscle, titin's stiffness exceeds ECM-stiffness.
source: This contrasts with studies that concluded that the passive stiffness of whole muscle fully resides in single fibers (titin) (Magid and Law, 1985) and also with work on cardiac muscle, where titin's stiffness exceeds ECM-stiffness (Granzier and Irving, 1995; Wu et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on cardiac muscle (Granzier and Irving, 1995; Wu et al., 2000).

claim: In fascioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD), titin-based stiffness is increased.
source: In fascioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) titin-based stiffness is increased (Lassche et al., 2013) and in cerebral palsy patients, an increase in titin-based passive stiffness has been implicated as well (Ottenheijm and Granzier, 2010; Fridén and Lieber, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing increased titin-based stiffness in FSHD (Lassche et al., 2013).

claim: In cerebral palsy patients, an increase in titin-based passive stiffness has been implicated.
source: In fascioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) titin-based stiffness is increased (Lassche et al., 2013) and in cerebral palsy patients, an increase in titin-based passive stiffness has been implicated as well (Ottenheijm and Granzier, 2010; Fridén and Lieber, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies implicating increased titin-based stiffness in cerebral palsy (Ottenheijm and Granzier, 2010; Fridén and Lieber, 2003).

claim: Diaphragm fibers in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) have a reduced titin-based stiffness.
source: In contrast, diaphragm fibers in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) have a reduced titin-based stiffness (Ottenheijm et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing reduced titin-based stiffness in COPD (Ottenheijm et al., 2006).

claim: A mouse model was created in which titin's stiffness was increased by shortening titin's molecular spring region through deletion of 47 PEVK exons (Ttn exon 112–158).
source: To aid in this work, a mouse model was created in which titin's stiffness was increased by shortening titin's molecular spring region. We targeted for deletion 47 PEVK exons (Ttn exon 112–158), referred to as the TtnΔ112-158 model.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the creation of the mouse model.

claim: The 47 targeted exons are all PEVK exons located in titin's I-band region.
source: The 47 targeted exons are all PEVK exons and their location in titin's I-band region is shown in Figure 1A and B.
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly and refers to Figure 1A and B for visual confirmation.

claim: The targeted exons are not expressed in the main cardiac titin isoform.
source: These exons are not expressed in the main cardiac titin isoform (Bang et al., 2001) and a skeletal-muscle-specific effect is expected.
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation support (Bang et al., 2001).

claim: A skeletal-muscle-specific effect is expected from the deletion.
source: These exons are not expressed in the main cardiac titin isoform (Bang et al., 2001) and a skeletal-muscle-specific effect is expected.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this expectation based on the exon expression pattern.

claim: The genotype distribution of mice born to heterozygous parents followed Mendelian genetics.
source: The genotype distribution of mice born to heterozygous parents followed Mendelian genetics (Figure 1C) and homozygous TtnΔ112-158 mice survived without an outwardly noticeable phenotype (oldest mice ~ 1 year).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly and refers to Figure 1C showing the distribution.

claim: Homozygous TtnΔ112-158 mice survived without an outwardly noticeable phenotype for up to approximately 1 year.
source: The genotype distribution of mice born to heterozygous parents followed Mendelian genetics (Figure 1C) and homozygous TtnΔ112-158 mice survived without an outwardly noticeable phenotype (oldest mice ~ 1 year).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the survival and phenotype observation.

claim: Homozygous TtnΔ112-158 mice had body weights indistinguishable from WT littermates at 60 days of life.
source: Homozygous TtnΔ112-158 mice had body weights indistinguishable from WT littermates at 60 days of life but as mice grew older a weight reduction appeared with two-way ANOVA measured across all ages revealing a significant effect of genotype on weight (Figure 1D top and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 1D and supplement.

claim: As TtnΔ112-158 mice grew older, a weight reduction appeared with two-way ANOVA revealing a significant effect of genotype on weight.
source: Homozygous TtnΔ112-158 mice had body weights indistinguishable from WT littermates at 60 days of life but as mice grew older a weight reduction appeared with two-way ANOVA measured across all ages revealing a significant effect of genotype on weight (Figure 1D top and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this with statistical analysis and figure references.

claim: TtnΔ112-158 mice had the same skeleton size as WT mice, as indicated by identical tibia lengths.
source: The TtnΔ112-158 mice had the same skeleton size, as suggested by their tibia lengths that were the same as that of WT mice (Figure 1D bottom, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with figure references.

claim: Full-length titin (T1) has a higher mobility in TtnΔ112-158 mice compared to WT mice.
source: TtnΔ112-158 muscle lysates also revealed T1 and T2 bands but, compared to WT lysates, T1 had a higher mobility in the TtnΔ112-158 mouse (Figure 1E), as expected from the exon deletion (representing a maximum of 181 kDa protein).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 1E showing the gel mobility.

claim: The mobility of T2 titin was unaffected in TtnΔ112-158 mice.
source: The mobility of T2 was unaffected (Figure 1E), also as expected because T2 of WT mice does not contain the targeted PEVK segment (Helmes et al., 1996).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 1E and citation (Helmes et al., 1996).

claim: No differences were found in titin expression in any of the studied muscle types between WT and TtnΔ112-158 mice.
source: In each muscle type, the total titin (T1 +T2) expression level was determined, relative to myosin heavy chain, and the amount of T1 relative to total titin. No differences were found in titin expression in any of the studied muscle types (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states no differences with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: RNA sequencing confirmed that PEVK exons 112–158 were absent in the TtnΔ112-158 transcript in all three muscle types studied.
source: RNA sequencing confirmed that the PEVK exons 112–158 were absent in the TtnΔ112-158 transcript, in all three muscle types (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 2B and source data.

claim: Only minimal differences outside the deleted region were found in titin transcript expression.
source: Only minimal differences outside the deleted region were found. In all muscle types, there was only consistent upregulation of Z-disk exons 12 and 13 and PEVK exon 159.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states minimal differences were found.

claim: Z-disk exons 12 and 13 and PEVK exon 159 were consistently upregulated in all muscle types of TtnΔ112-158 mice.
source: Only minimal differences outside the deleted region were found. In all muscle types, there was only consistent upregulation of Z-disk exons 12 and 13 and PEVK exon 159.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states these exons were upregulated.

claim: The PEVK segment was reduced from approximately 1600 to approximately 420 residues in TtnΔ112-158 mice.
source: The average transcript size was determined by multiplying the measured PSI for each exon by the number of residues encoded by the exon, which resulted in 1611, 1538 and 1613 PEVK residues for WT and 421, 429 and 412 for TtnΔ112-158 transcript, in diaphragm, EDL and soleus muscle, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific calculated values for PEVK residues.

claim: The three muscle types (diaphragm, EDL, and soleus) are highly similar in titin exon expression in both WT and TtnΔ112-158 mice.
source: It is worthwhile noting how similar the three muscle types are, both in WT (Figure 2B top) and TtnΔ112-158 mice (Figure 2B bottom).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly notes the similarity with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: In both diaphragm and EDL muscles of TtnΔ112-158 mice, the extension of the PEVK segment was reduced.
source: Figure 3A shows sample images. In both Diaphragm and EDL muscles of TtnΔ112-158 mice the extension (z) of the PEVK segment was reduced (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 3B showing the measurements.

claim: The titin-based stiffness of TtnΔ112-158 mice is predicted to be greatly increased compared to WT.
source: The insets of Figure 3C reveal that, compared to WT, the titin-based stiffness of TtnΔ112-158 mice is predicted to be greatly increased.
evidence: The manuscript states this prediction based on wormlike chain modeling shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In all three muscle types, passive tension increased much more steeply with sarcomere length in TtnΔ112-158 muscles compared to WT.
source: The obtained passive tension- SL relations are given in Figure 4. In all three muscle types, passive tension increased much more steeply with SL in the TtnΔ112-158 muscles.
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 4 showing the measurements.

claim: Passive stiffness is increased approximately 5-10 fold in TtnΔ112-158 mice compared to WT.
source: From these data, the average passive stiffness (slope of tension – sarcomere length relation) in the sarcomere length range 2.45–2.75 μm was calculated. The results showed a several-fold increased passive stiffness in TtnΔ112-158 muscles (insets of Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript states several-fold increase with Figure 4 insets showing approximately 5-10 fold increases.

claim: Skinning had little effect on the passive tension of muscle in both WT and TtnΔ112-158 mice.
source: Passive tensions measured before and after skinning reveal no skinning-induced difference in passive tension, a result found in both genotypes (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 5A and B.

claim: The KCl/KI sensitive tension of skinned whole muscle is likely titin-based.
source: The KCl/KI sensitive tension was similar in magnitude to that of single fibers, as was the stiffness in the 2.45–2.75 μm sarcomere length range (Figure 5C). Thus, it is likely that the extraction sensitive tension of skinned whole muscle is titin-based and that the extraction-insensitive tension is ECM-based.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on comparison with single fiber data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The extraction-insensitive tension is ECM-based.
source: Thus, it is likely that the extraction sensitive tension of skinned whole muscle is titin-based and that the extraction-insensitive tension is ECM-based.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on the extraction experiments.

claim: The titin-based and ECM-based tension of EDL 5th toe muscle were both significantly higher in TtnΔ112-158 muscle.
source: The titin-based and ECM-based tension of EDL 5th toe muscle were both significantly higher in TtnΔ112-158 muscle (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: The titin-based passive stiffness in the 2.45–2.75 μm sarcomere length range was increased approximately 5 fold in TtnΔ112-158 muscle.
source: The titin-based passive stiffness in the 2.45–2.75 μm sarcomere length range was increased ~5 fold (Figure 5D, inset).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 5D inset.

claim: Within the physiological sarcomere length range of skeletal muscle, titin is the dominant determinant of passive stiffness in both WT and TtnΔ112-158 mice.
source: The ECM stiffness was increased as well but its magnitude remained much below the stiffness of titin. Thus, passive TtnΔ112-158 skeletal muscles are much stiffer, which largely can be accounted for by increased titin stiffness.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on the comparison of titin and ECM stiffness measurements.

claim: No genotype effect on maximal active tension was found in any muscle type studied.
source: The maximal active tensions for all studied muscle types are in Figure 6B. The different muscle types generated different active tension levels in WT animals, as expected because these muscles express different myosin isoforms that impact force generation (Schiaffino and Reggiani, 2011). However, no genotype effect on maximal active tension was found (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 6B and citation (Schiaffino and Reggiani, 2011).

claim: The time required to generate half-maximal tetanic tension was significantly reduced in all muscle types of TtnΔ112-158 mice.
source: A significant genotype effect was found, and a multiple comparison analysis revealed a significantly reduced time to half-maximal tension in all muscle types of TtnΔ112-158 mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: No genotype effect on myosin isoform composition was found in the three muscle types studied.
source: To evaluate whether this can be explained by a fiber type switch in TtnΔ112-158 mice, a myosin-isoform analysis was performed in the 3 muscle types but no genotype effect was found (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: The average running speed and average running distance per 24 hours of TtnΔ112-158 mice were not different from WT mice in free-wheel running.
source: However, the average running speed and the average running distance (per 24 hr) of TtnΔ112-158 mice were not different from WT mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: No genotype effect was found in maximal running speed, total distance covered, or oxygen consumption at maximal running speed in metabolic treadmill testing.
source: Even when mice were pushed to their extreme, no genotype effect was found in the maximal running speed and the total distance covered (Figure 7B, left and middle). The oxygen consumption (VO2) at the maximal running speed was also not different (Figure 7B, right).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: The diaphragm strain amplitude did not vary between TtnΔ112-158 and WT mice.
source: Before perfusion, ultrasound imaging was used to measure during the respiration cycle, the diaphragm strain amplitude (fractional shortening of the muscle fibers during inspiration). Diaphragm strain amplitude did not vary between TtnΔ112-158 and WT mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 8A.

claim: TtnΔ112-158 mice had a significantly reduced sarcomere length both during expiration and inspiration in the diaphragm.
source: Results reveal that the TtnΔ112-158 mice had a significantly reduced sarcomere length both during expiration and inspiration (Figure 8B); the physiological sarcomere length range of the diaphragm was 2.85 μm to 2.22 μm in WT mice but only 2.37 μm to 1.88 μm in TtnΔ112-158 mice.
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with specific values and reference to Figure 8B.

claim: TtnΔ112-158 mice had shorter sarcomere lengths in stretched as well as shortened EDL and soleus muscles.
source: Figure 8C reveals in TtnΔ112-158 mice shorter sarcomere lengths in stretched as well as shortened EDL and soleus muscles.
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 8C.

claim: Muscles of TtnΔ112-158 mice have shifted their physiological sarcomere lengths to shorter lengths in the diaphragm as well as peripheral muscles.
source: Overall, the results (schematically shown in Figure 8D) support that muscles of the TtnΔ112-158 mice have shifted their physiological sarcomere lengths to shorter lengths, in the diaphragm as well as peripheral muscles.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on the measurements shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Fiber lengths in TtnΔ112-158 mice were significantly increased by 13.5%.
source: To explore the mechanisms underlying the shorter sarcomere length working range, single fibers were dissected from end-to-end in chemically fixed muscles (Materials and methods). Fiber lengths in the TtnΔ112-158 mice were significantly increased by 13.5% (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with specific percentage and figure reference.

claim: There was a significant and large increase of approximately 30% in the number of sarcomeres in all examined TtnΔ112-158 muscles.
source: The sarcomere length of the dissected fibers was also determined (laser diffraction) and by dividing the measured fiber length by the obtained sarcomere length, the total number of sarcomeres along the fibers was calculated. This revealed a significant and large increase (~30%) in the number of sarcomeres in all examined TtnΔ112-158 muscles (Figure 9).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with specific percentage and reference to Figure 9.

claim: Most TtnΔ112-158 muscle types had a significantly increased muscle weight relative to WT controls.
source: To determine whether the increased number of sarcomeres resulted in increased muscle weights, a range of muscle types were studied, including the diaphragm, EDL and soleus muscles. Muscle weights were determined at 60, 80, 183 (6 mo) and 274 (9 mo) days of life. Most TtnΔ112-158 muscle types had a significantly increased muscle weight, relative to WT controls (Figure 10A–C and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to figures.

claim: The cross-sectional area of muscles was not increased in TtnΔ112-158 mice.
source: Since the cross-sectional area of muscles was not increased (Figure 10D) it is likely that the increased weight in TtnΔ112-158 muscles is largely accounted for by longitudinal muscle growth.
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with reference to Figure 10D.

claim: The increased weight in TtnΔ112-158 muscles is likely largely accounted for by longitudinal muscle growth.
source: Since the cross-sectional area of muscles was not increased (Figure 10D) it is likely that the increased weight in TtnΔ112-158 muscles is largely accounted for by longitudinal muscle growth.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on the lack of cross-sectional area increase.

claim: The thin filament length was significantly reduced from 1165 nm in WT to 1102 nm in TtnΔ112-158 diaphragm mice.
source: The thin filament length was therefore measured, by localizing the thin filament capping protein Tmod4 in diaphragm muscle (Materials and methods). The thin filament length was significantly reduced (Figure 11A), from 1165 nm in WT to 1102 nm in TtnΔ112-158 mice.
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with specific values and reference to Figure 11A.

claim: Within the working range, WT sarcomeres developed on average 91% of the maximal force and TtnΔ112-158 sarcomeres 96% of the maximal force.
source: The average force within the working range was calculated (using the predicted forces at 0.05 μm SL increments). Within the working range, WT sarcomeres developed on average 91% of the maximal force and TtnΔ112-158 sarcomeres 96% of the maximal force.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific calculated percentages.

claim: Due to the reduced thin filament length, there appears to be little downside for active force development despite the reduction in physiological sarcomere length working range in TtnΔ112-158 mice.
source: Thus, although the reduction in the physiological sarcomere length working range is quite large in TtnΔ112-158 mice, due to the reduced thin filament length there appears to be little downside for active force development.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on the force-sarcomere length analysis.

claim: The upregulation of Z-disk exons 12 and 13 is triggered by the increased titin-based tension in TtnΔ112-158 mice to mechanically strengthen the Z-disk region.
source: However, considering that there is no fiber type switch in the muscles that were studied in TtnΔ112-158 mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), it is unlikely that the upregulation of exons 12 and 13 reflects a change towards fiber types with wider Z-disks. Instead, we propose that the upregulation of exons 12 and 13 is triggered by the increased titin-based tension in TtnΔ112-158 mice, in order to mechanically strengthen this critical region of the sarcomere when titin's stiffness is high.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this mechanism based on the data and reasoning.

claim: The adaptation in the physiological sarcomere length range of TtnΔ112-158 mice is remarkably effective at normalizing passive stiffness.
source: That this shift is functionally important can be evaluated by plotting the average passive stiffness of titin in the physiological sarcomere length range. This reveals an identical passive stiffness in the two genotypes (see Figure 12). Thus, the adaptation in the physiological sarcomere length range of the TtnΔ112-158 mice is remarkably effective at normalizing passive stiffness.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on the analysis shown in Figure 12.

claim: The TtnΔ112-158 mice are likely to have a lower body fat content based on increased muscle weights combined with reduced body weight and normal body size.
source: The increased muscles weights, combined with the reduced body weight and normal body size (revealed by the normal tibia lengths, discussed above), suggests that the TtnΔ112-158 mice are likely to have a lower body fat content.
evidence: The manuscript suggests this based on the combination of measurements.

claim: At the macroscopic scale of a whole muscle contracting at L0, the titin unfolding/refolding mechanism is unlikely to significantly add to the level of tetanic tension.
source: It is possible that the refolding mechanism is not active because passive forces at L0 are too low, in both genotypes. Perhaps, at longer lengths sufficient levels of unfolding might take place, due to the higher passive tensions, and the mechanism is operational. Presently we conclude that at the macroscopic scale of a whole muscle contracting at L0, the titin unfolding/refolding mechanism is unlikely to significantly add to the level of tetanic tension.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on the active tension measurements.

claim: The more rapid force development in TtnΔ112-158 muscle is speculated to be due to the higher passive tension increasing the thick filament ON state, which accelerates force generation when a muscle is stimulated.
source: Because no fiber type switch was found in TtnΔ112-158 muscles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) it is unlikely that this increased speed of force development is due to the expression of faster fiber types. Instead, we speculate that this more rapid force development is due to the higher passive tension in TtnΔ112-158 muscle that increases the thick filament ON state and that this accelerates force generation when a muscle is stimulated.
evidence: The manuscript speculates this mechanism based on the data.

claim: In TtnΔ112-158 mice, the nebulin-free distal segment of the thin filament is speculated to be reduced in length in response to the shift in the sarcomere length working range.
source: Considering that the thin filament contains a distal nebulin-free segment (Littlefield and Fowler, 2008), we speculate that in TtnΔ112-158 mice this nebulin-free distal segment is reduced in length, in response to the shift in the sarcomere length working range.
evidence: The manuscript speculates this mechanism based on the thin filament length data and citation (Littlefield and Fowler, 2008).

claim: Normalizing function through the addition of approximately 30% sarcomeres is energetically costly, as suggested by the reduced weight of TtnΔ112-158 mice.
source: Normalizing function through the addition of ~30% sarcomeres is energetically costly, as suggested by the reduced weight of the TtnΔ112-158 mice (Figure 1D), and ultimately might be detrimental.
evidence: The manuscript suggests this based on the body weight data.

claim: The TtnΔ112-158 model provides a unique opportunity to test the effects of altered titin-based tension on active muscle function.
source: The TtnΔ112-158 model also provides a unique opportunity to test the effects of altered titin-based tension on active muscle function.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this opportunity.

claim: Titin might store elastic energy by unfolding Ig domains in passive muscle and generate forces through their refolding during contraction that add to active force.
source: For example, titin might store elastic energy by unfolding Ig domains in passive muscle. Through their refolding during contraction, titin might generate forces that add to the active force (Eckels et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a proposed mechanism (Eckels et al., 2018).

claim: An alternative mechanism consists of titin-based effects on thick filament structure that contribute to activating the thick filament.
source: An alternative mechanism consists of titin-based effects on thick filament structure that contribute to activating the thick filament (Piazzesi et al., 2018; Fusi et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites proposed mechanisms (Piazzesi et al., 2018; Fusi et al., 2016).

claim: Within the physiological length range of skeletal muscle, titin's contribution to whole muscle stiffness is dominant, analogous to cardiac muscle.
source: Within the physiological length range of skeletal muscle, however, titin's contribution to whole muscle stiffness is dominant. This is analogous to cardiac muscle where titin also dominates within the physiological sarcomere length (Granzier and Irving, 1995; Wu et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript concludes this and draws an analogy to cardiac muscle with citations (Granzier and Irving, 1995; Wu et al., 2000).

claim: An advantage of titin dominating passive stiffness is that this allows for rapid regulation through intracellular signaling mechanisms that post-translationally modify titin's molecular spring region.
source: An advantage of titin dominating passive stiffness is that this allows for rapid regulation through intracellular signaling mechanisms that post-translationally modify titin's molecular spring region (Hidalgo and Granzier, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript states this advantage with citation support (Hidalgo and Granzier, 2013).

claim: At sarcomere lengths at or beyond the physiological range limit, the ECM stiffness greatly increases and functions as a brake on the movement range of muscle.
source: This does not mean that the ECM is unimportant for longitudinal stiffness. At sarcomere lengths at or beyond the physiological range limit, the ECM stiffness greatly increases and functions as a brake on the movement range of muscle.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the role of ECM at extreme lengths.

claim: The targeting strategy used homologous recombination to replace exons 112–158 (chr2:76,839,202–76,867,333).
source: The targeting strategy used homologous recombination to replace exons 112–158 (chr2:76,839,202–76,867,333) with the exon numbers from orthologous human titin exons.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the targeting strategy with genomic coordinates.

claim: The TtnΔ112-158 deletion corresponds to a deletion of 47 PEVK exons, encoding 1586 amino acids or 181.7 kDa.
source: The TtnΔ112-158 deletion corresponds to a deletion of 47 PEVK exons, encoding 1586 amino acids or 181.7 kDa.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific details about the deletion size.

claim: The passive stiffness of titin and ECM were both significantly increased in TtnΔ112-158 EDL muscle, but the titin stiffness far exceeded the ECM stiffness, approximately 5-fold in WT and approximately 10-fold in TtnΔ112-158 muscle.
source: The stiffness of titin and ECM were both significantly increased in TtnΔ112-158 EDL muscle but the titin stiffness far exceeded the ECM stiffness, ~5-fold in WT and ~10-fold in TtnΔ112-158 muscle (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript states this explicitly with specific fold-changes and figure reference.

claim: The WT mice operate on the descending limb and part of the plateau of the force-sarcomere length relation, while TtnΔ112-158 muscle starts out on the plateau and shortens on the ascending limb.
source: The WT mice operate on the descending limb and part of the plateau, but in contrast, the TtnΔ112-158 muscle starts out on the plateau and shortens on the ascending limb.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the different operating ranges on the force-SL curve.

claim: The physiological sarcomere length range of the diaphragm was 2.85 μm to 2.22 μm in WT mice but only 2.37 μm to 1.88 μm in TtnΔ112-158 mice.
